opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. Some slowdown is natural as you grow. When you're a small team, everyone knows the whole codebase and every customer, so decisions happen in a hallway conversation. Once you have thousands of people and many enterprise customers depending on you, you can't move the same way. A change that breaks something is a much bigger deal, so you add reviews, testing, compatibility guarantees, and some of that friction is actually the right call.

But a lot of slowdown isn't inherent. It comes from how you organize. The thing I try to watch for is whether teams can still own something end to end. If shipping a feature requires coordinating across five groups, each with its own priorities, everything slows to the pace of the slowest dependency. So we try to keep teams small, give them a clear area and real autonomy, and invest heavily in shared infrastructure, internal platforms, CI, and good abstractions, so each team isn't reinventing those things or waiting on someone else.

The other piece is culture. Engineers at a big company can start optimizing for not making mistakes instead of for learning quickly. In research, and in the early days of Spark, you learned by putting something out, seeing how people used it, and iterating. I try to keep that alive by launching things early as previews, being upfront that they're experimental, and getting real users on them before we've polished every edge. That way you get the speed of feedback without putting your core product at risk.

And honestly, staying close to the technology helps. If leadership is still looking at code, talking to users, and trying the product, you notice much faster when the process is getting in the way. Most slowdown creeps in gradually, so you have to keep pushing back on it.

r001.rationale: The response says small autonomous teams can reduce organizational friction, but it does not state that a core group of people is exempt from the slowdown of operating at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a real thing, and I think anyone who's gone from a startup to a company with a few thousand people has felt it. The honest answer is that some of the slowdown is actually good and some of it is just entropy, and the job is telling those apart.

The good kind is that when you have thousands of customers running production workloads on your platform, you really do need to be careful. At Databricks, if we ship something that breaks a customer's pipeline at 2 a.m., that's a very different situation than when it was six of us at Berkeley pushing a new Spark release and seeing who complained on the mailing list. So a lot of the process that shows up, the testing, the staged rollouts, the reviews, it's there because the cost of a mistake went up. I don't think of that as a slowdown so much as the price of actually mattering to people.

The bad kind is when decisions start requiring too many people to agree, or when teams stop talking directly to users because there's a layer of product managers and account teams in between. That's the thing I try to push back on hardest. One of the ways we've tried to handle it is to keep teams small and give them real ownership of a problem end to end, so a group working on, say, serverless compute or on something in the AI stack can move more or less the way a startup would. The other thing is just insisting that engineers still sit with customers and look at real workloads. A lot of the best things we've built came from someone noticing a pattern across customer problems, not from a planning cycle.

And I'd say the research side helps too. Part of why I've kept one foot in academia is that it's a good forcing function for thinking about what the right answer is in five years rather than what the roadmap says for next quarter. Big companies are very good at optimizing the thing they already do. They're much worse at noticing that the thing itself should change. So you have to deliberately carve out space for that, because the default gravity of a large organization pulls toward incremental work.

r001.rationale: The response says small, autonomous teams can move more like a startup, but it does not state that a core group is exempt from the slowdown of operating at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that, as the company grows, more things require coordination. When you’re a small team, everyone has the context, and you can just make a decision and try something. At a larger company, even a fairly simple change can involve several teams with different priorities.

So I think a lot about how to give small teams enough ownership that they can move independently. You want clear interfaces and clear goals, without requiring everyone to agree on every implementation detail. And you want to preserve the ability to experiment—to have someone build a prototype and show that an idea works before turning it into a big planning exercise.

Some slowdown is also the consequence of having customers who depend on you. You can’t break things in the same way you could early on. The challenge is to put that care into the parts that need it while keeping exploration fast.

r001.rationale: The response discusses giving small teams ownership to move independently, but does not say that a core group of people is exempt from the slowdown of operating at scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that, as the company grows, you can’t be involved in every decision. If everything has to go through you, you become the source of the slowdown. So you have to build teams that can make good decisions independently, with enough shared context about what you’re trying to accomplish.

There are also things that genuinely get harder at scale. A change might affect a lot of customers, and you have to be more careful about reliability and compatibility. But I don’t think that means everything has to move slowly. You want small teams that can experiment quickly, and then a clear path for taking something that works and making it broadly available. A lot of the work is figuring out which decisions need coordination and which ones you can just let a team run with.

r001.rationale: The response says teams should make decisions independently, but does not state that a core group of people is exempt from the slowdown of operating at scale.
